extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy; scholars studying ethical theory (Schopenhauer)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition of what constitutes moral worth in actions: a set of axioms about motive and will, classification of fundamental springs of conduct, and the claim that compassion (identification with others' weal/woe) is the sole true moral incentive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of moral worth (absence of egoistic motives)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral value of an act is determined by the absence of all self-interested (egoistic) motives; the moral value is lowered by disclosure of an accessory selfish incentive and entirely destroyed if the incentive stood alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Chapter IV: 'The absence of all egoistic motives is thus the =Criterion= of an action of moral value.' Acts of voluntary justice and unselfish loving-kindness qualify only insofar as they reject and exclude self-interested motives. Malice/cruelty are excepted as not qualifying because they make others' suffering the end in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal sign of moral worth — approval of conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct having real moral worth leaves behind a certain self-satisfaction called the approval of conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an internal, subjective mark distinguishing morally worthy acts from injustice or cruelty, which involve secret self-condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: External sign of moral worth — approval of disinterested witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: An accidental/external sign: genuinely moral acts win the approval and respect of disinterested witnesses, whereas immoral acts incur their disapproval and contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a secondary, corroborating indicator of moral worth in empirical investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental axioms about action and motive (1–9)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of nine propositions presupposed as axioms for the analysis of moral action and motive (e.g., no action without a sufficient motive; motive implies sense of weal and woe; every action relates to a being susceptible of weal and woe; egoistic actions have the doer's weal/woe as ultimate object; moral worth and egoism exclude each other; moral significance lies in effect upon others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists and uses these axioms (numbered (1)–(9)) to deduce that only actions whose ultimate incentive is the weal/woe of another (not the agent) can have moral worth. Key stated axioms include: (1) no action without sufficient motive; (3) whatever moves the Will implies sense of weal and woe; (6) actions whose ultimate object is the agent's weal/woe are egoistic; (8) egoism and moral worth absolutely exclude each other; (9) moral significance can only lie in effect produced upon others (given elimination of duties to self).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral significance determined by relation to others' welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Because alleged duties toward ourselves are eliminated, the moral significance of conduct can only lie in the effect produced upon others: its relation to others is alone what lends it moral worth or worthlessness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shifts the criterion of morality away from self-regarding motives and toward consequences for other persons' weal and woe (see axiom (9)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion as the sole true moral incentive
rubrics_metrics.description: Compassion — the direct participation in the sufferings of another, leading to sympathetic assistance — is the only motive that can give actions genuine moral worth; only insofar as an action springs from compassion does it have moral value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as a proved conclusion: 'It is this Compassion alone which is the real basis of all =voluntary= justice and all =genuine= loving-kindness.' The text explains that compassion makes another's weal/woe directly constitute the agent's motive by identifying the other with the agent (removing the difference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three fundamental springs of human conduct (classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: All motives arise from one of three springs: (a) Egoism — desires the weal of the self; (b) Malice — desires the woe of others; (c) Compassion — desires the weal of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tripartite classification is used as an explanatory schema: since moral actions cannot arise from (a) or (b) (by axiom (8)), they must arise from (c). The text notes two springs may operate together but every human act is referable to one or other of these.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of Egoism
rubrics_metrics.description: Egoism is the chief, fundamental incentive: the urgent impulse to exist and to exist under the best circumstances; actions whose ultimate object is the agent's own weal/woe are egoistic and thus lack moral worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Egoism is described as limitless, underlying most human actions; even religious or rule-following behaviour can be egoistic if ultimately motivated by the agent's own weal (e.g., rewards, fear of punishment, reputation, self-perfection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of Malice
rubrics_metrics.description: Malice is the desire for others' woe and can develop to the utmost cruelty; conduct springing from malice is morally worthless and in principle opposite to compassion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malice/ill-will may arise from envy, spite, or pleasure in others' suffering; distinguished from egoism because its ultimate purpose is others' harm rather than the agent's benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification mechanism: how compassion operates
rubrics_metrics.description: For another's weal/woe to influence my will as my own, I must 'identify' with him by means of the mental picture/knowledge of him, so that the difference between myself and him is practically effaced and I 'suffer with him'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats this identification as the psychological/metaphysical process enabling compassion to be an immediate motive; it underpins the claim that compassion can directly move the will in the same way as self-regarding motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of religious/metaphysical incentives as genuinely moral
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions performed out of belief in divine reward or fear of divine punishment are still egoistic motives and therefore do not constitute morality of the heart; such incentives amount to self-interest (a 'bill of exchange' payable later) rather than genuine unselfishness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that though religious inducements may secure lawful behaviour, they fail to produce genuine moral worth because the agent's motive remains self-regarding (e.g., expectation of reward, avoidance of punishment, concern for reputation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetry of sympathy: direct sympathy arises from suffering, not well-being
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct sympathy (compassion) is awakened by another's suffering, want or need (positive stimuli), but not directly by another's well-being, which is negative (absence of pain) and therefore leaves us indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained by the positive nature of pain vs. the negative nature of pleasure/satisfaction; this principle is used to explain why compassion responds mainly to distress and not to others' happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical confirmation requirement for moral claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical science must proceed empirically: we must search experience for actions of voluntary justice and unselfish loving-kindness and then account for them by identifying their motives (not rely on a priori constructs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text rejects purely a priori moral constructions (Categorical Imperative etc.) and insists the basis of Ethics must be reached empirically by tracing motives to their ultimate sources in human nature.
